title: LO: Write learning objectives and success criteria
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart examines how teachers write learning objectives and success criteria, arguing that the practice is often overcomplicated and confused. He begins by warning against conflating learning with performance, noting that learning happens over time rather than in a single lesson. He argues for clarity of intention, rooted in a well-sequenced curriculum rather than lifted national-curriculum statements, and for objectives that describe intended learning rather than tasks, drawing on Shirley Clarke and Peps McCrea. His central distinction is between closed objectives, where success is binary and criteria take the form of procedural steps, and open objectives, where success is a continuum and criteria act as a toolkit, illustrated with maths and suspense writing. He then critiques the inspection-driven habit of displaying objectives on a slide, recommends co-constructing criteria through modelling and examples, and warns against tasks that drift from what was modelled or that multiply objectives through over-differentiation.
points: Hart argues that single-lesson objectives invite the conflation of learning with performance, because children completing the set work is not evidence that learning has happened.
National curriculum statements are not precise enough to bring clarity to an hour of teaching; objectives should come from a scheme of work with a clear end point.
Closed objectives call for procedural success criteria ('rules'), while open objectives call for a toolkit of choices, and forcing procedural criteria onto writing misses its effect on the reader.
Sharing an objective on a slide at the start of a lesson can mean nothing to children; examples, non-examples and narrated modelling communicate more.
He recommends one objective with layered challenge rather than several differentiated tasks, which he calls a workload nightmare that quietly creates different objectives.
quotes: In short, no. Learning happens over time; the result of multiple, iterative interactions with the content within and across units of work. Yet we have learning objectives for individual lessons and and are happy to tell ourselves that children have achieved our learning objective if they complete the work that we set.
If we are going to be able to portray curriculum content in a way that renders it comprehensible to naive minds, we have to be clear. And this starts with clarity of intention.
But the national curriculum is not a scheme of work. It simply details what children should be taught by the end of each key stage, sometimes split by year group as a guide.
Closed objectives are absolute. Success is binary; children can either know it or they don’t yet. They can either do it or they can’t yet.
Writing is about the effect on the reader, not the mechanical use of expanded noun phrases, fronted adverbial and relative clauses. Is there a place for learning these? Yes!

A slide with an objective and a list of criteria at the beginning of a lesson could quite easily mean nothing to a group of children. Done badly, they might never be recorded anywhere and end up in the land of wind and ghosts because of the transient word effect.
Differentiating tasks several ways is a workload nightmare. It can also manifest as several learning objectives.
